title: Proof pages for an architecture studio
metaTitle: Proof pages that show an architecture decision
excerpt: A project page should show the constraint, the decision, and the built work. Photographs with no decision are decoration. End on how a similar client can start a conversation.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, a calm view that still needs a decision before it can prove a project.
caption: A quiet shoreline. A project page still has to name what was hard. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first lines of a project page say?
faqs.answer: The constraint, then the decision. A steep site, a party wall, a heritage rule, or a budget that killed the first scheme. Then the move you made. The photographs come after that sentence, so the reader knows what the picture is arguing.

faqs.question: How long should a project page be?
faqs.answer: Long enough to show one constraint, one decision, and the built result. A short caption under a reel is not a proof page. A monograph that never says what was refused is not one either. Stop when a similar client could explain the job to someone else.

faqs.question: Where should the page send the reader?
faqs.answer: Into a project conversation, with a hint of who it is for. If the job was a tight alteration, say that a similar alteration can start with the address and a note on what is failing. Do not end on a credits list and a void.

markdown:
An architecture studio case study page should show the constraint, the decision, and the built work, in that order. A client judging taste before competence is looking for judgment. Photographs with no decision attached are decoration.

End the page on how a similar client can start a project conversation. The proof is not finished when the last image is beautiful. It is finished when the next person knows whether their site belongs here, and what to do about it.

## The constraint, before the gallery

Open with the limit that made the project a project. A lane too narrow for the crane you wanted. A heritage overlay that kept the front room. A budget that removed the second storey. A brief that asked for a grandparent and a teenager to share a house without sharing a staircase. One constraint, named in the first paragraph, is enough. A list of every difficulty becomes a complaint.

Write it the way you would brief a new staff member. Facts, not atmosphere. If a reader cannot tell what was hard, the later photographs will be admired and forgotten. Taste without a limit is how every office's gallery starts to look the same.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) talks about showing how a piece of work was made, and about evidence a reader can check. For a product review, that evidence includes what was tested and photographs of the work. A project page is the same kind of account. The constraint is the test. The photograph should show the result of a decision, not a weather condition.

Say what you were given. The existing plan, the planning rule, the client's non-negotiable. Readers trust a page that admits the starting point. A page that begins at the finished glow implies the building arrived by taste alone.

## The decision, in one place

After the constraint, one paragraph on the move. "We kept the front rooms and put the new stair in the old service wing." "We split the garden into two levels so the living room could open without a tall retaining wall on the street." The sentence should be repeatable. If you need a diagram to make it true, put the diagram next to the sentence. Do not make the reader reconstruct the plan from adjectives.

Say what you refused, when that refusal is the judgment. The extra bedroom that would have killed the courtyard. The glass corner that the budget could not detail properly. Refusal is often the proof. Clients who are judging competence want to see that you can stop, not only that you can add.

Keep credits nearby but not first. Collaborators, the builder, the photographer. They belong on the page. They do not replace the decision. A block of logos at the top tells a peer who else was in the room. It does not tell a client what you did.

If the project is not built, label the drawings as drawings. A proof page can include an unbuilt scheme when you are honest about its status. It cannot dress a render as a photograph. The client who is about to spend years with you is watching for that honesty more than for the tree species in the visualization.

## Photographs that carry the decision

Choose frames that make the sentence visible. If the decision was a low window to a brick lane, show that window and that lane, in the light the room actually gets. If the decision was a joint between old plaster and new timber, show the joint. A dusk elevation with the lights on can be lovely and still fail to prove the move.

Sequence the images in the order of the argument. Approach. The hard moment. The room that resulted. A detail that would have been expensive to get wrong. Then stop. Twenty similar interiors teach the reader that you own a photographer. Six images tied to sentences teach them that you can decide.

Write the caption as part of the proof, not as a filename. "North light on the new stair, kept clear of the party wall" is a caption. "IMG_2044" and "Interior" are not. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats images as content, under the principle that information should be perceivable. A text alternative should carry the fact in the picture: what room, what is happening, what a person who cannot see it still needs to know. "Beautiful architecture" fails that, and it also fails the client who can see.

Do not rely on a fullscreen crop with the words burned into the image file. Those words disappear for anyone using a reader, and they cannot be edited when the sentence improves. Keep the type in the page. Keep the photograph as the photograph.

Thomas Bewick, a public Hanabi project, is an editorial site where heritage craft is shown with context rather than as a floating picture. The lesson transfers. A building page that separates the image from the decision has chosen atmosphere over proof.

## Drawings, models, and the words beside them

Plans earn their place when the decision is spatial. A before-and-after plan of an alteration often explains more than a third interior. Label the rooms in language the client uses. If the plan is tiny on a phone, it is not doing the job. Offer a crop of the relevant bay, or a simple diagram redrawn for the screen, and keep the full drawing available.

Sections matter when height was the constraint. A flood level, a neighbor's outlook, a stair clearance. Show the line. A render that hides the section is asking the reader to trust the mood.

Models and material boards can sit in the middle of the story, as evidence of a choice, not as a scrapbook. "We tested three stair materials and kept the one the builder could finish in the existing opening." That is a decision. A grid of samples with no sentence is a Pinterest export.

Mark north, or the street, if orientation is the point. Do not mark every dimension. This is not the construction set. The construction set is what the client pays for later. The page is what helps a similar client recognize their problem.

## What a page without a decision is

A reel of rooms, a map pin, and a list of materials is a lookbook. It can live on a social feed. It is a weak proof page, because a client cannot tell what was difficult or what you would do again. Screenshots of a drawing set with no annotation have the same problem. The reader sees that software was used. They do not see judgment.

Cut images that do not change the argument. If two photographs show the same corner in different weather, keep the one that shows the decision. Empty beauty is the beach at sunrise problem: pleasant, and silent about the work.

Do not inflate the result. No invented savings, no invented timelines, no quotes you do not have permission to print. A plain account of the constraint and the move is stronger than a testimonial you polished. If a client will say a sentence in their own words and you may use it, keep it short and specific. If you are unsure, leave it out.

Avoid a template so rigid that every project pretends to have the same drama. Some jobs are quiet. Say so. "The constraint was ordinary: a dark middle room. The decision was a new opening to the side court." Quiet and specific beats a false turning point.

## End on a similar client

The last block is the handoff. Name who this proof is for. "If you have a terrace that needs another bedroom without losing the garden, start a project conversation with the address and a few photographs." That sentence does more than a generic contact button, because it tells the wrong client to look at a different project.

Link back to the matching service, if you have one, and to one related project. Three links, not thirty. The reader should leave with a next page, not a maze.

Keep a single action label, the same one as the rest of the site. Start a project. Say what happens after they write, in whatever window your office truly keeps. The proof page is a bad place to invent a new form.

If you want to see the same standard applied to public projects, look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful ones let you retell the constraint. Hanabi designs and builds marketing sites where the project story is text plus pictures, not a locked slideshow. You should be able to correct a caption when the building teaches you a better sentence.

## How a reader finds the next proof

One strong page is not a library. The reader who finishes a house alteration needs a way to the next alteration, or back to the list of work, without guessing which menu item means projects. Labels are the map. "Work," "Houses," and "Start a project" are jobs. "Explore" is not.

That map is [navigation for an architecture studio](/blog/navigation-for-an-architecture-studio). Write the proof so it can be found by the kind of client it serves. A brilliant page buried under a poetic menu still fails the person who was ready to talk.
